text:
**1/** Banks promise to grow your money. Savings circles — tandas, susus, hui, equbs, chit funds — promise something different: you *will* save. Centuries later, they're still winning on the things small savers actually need. 🧵

**2/** The mechanism: a group contributes a fixed amount every cycle. The pot goes to one member each round — by set order, lottery, or bid — until everyone has taken it. No branch, no paperwork, no app required.

**3/** Why it works 1/ — commitment. A bank balance is one tap from being spent. A circle payment is gone the moment you make it; you only recover it by staying in. Kenyan fieldwork ("You Can't Save Alone," Gugerty 2007) found this is exactly why people join.

**4/** 2/ — social collateral replaces credit scores. Miss a payment and the penalty isn't a fee; it's face and future access. Anderson & Baland (2002) found married women in Kenyan circles saved measurably more than non-members — the group shields cash from daily claims on it.

**5/** 3/ — a lump sum on day one. Ten friends × $100/month = a $1,000 pot every month. An early taker effectively gets an interest-free ~$900 loan, no collateral, no credit history. Banks can't serve people without scores — and 1.4B adults still have no bank account at all (World Bank Findex).

**6/** 4/ — fees don't scale. On small balances, banks often cost more than the money earns: ~$25–35 per overdraft in the US, plus monthly maintenance unless minimums are met. A circle charges exactly $0 and happily handles $5 contributions.

**7/** 5/ — it runs on relationships, not branches. That's why circles thrive where banks don't reach: market traders, migrant workers, villages. And group saving stays common even among people who *have* accounts.

**8/** The honest catch: no deposit insurance. One defaulter mid-cycle, or an organizer who vanishes, sinks it. That's why circles work best small, among people you know, with the rotation set publicly — and why Kenyan chamas now keep records and move money over mobile payments.

**9/** Even regulators hedge: India licenses chit funds under the Chit Funds Act (1982). Informal ≠ illegal — it just means enforcement comes from reputation instead of courts.

**10/** Verdict: banks are safer vaults. Circles are better coaches. For small, regular savers they deliver discipline, zero fees, and score-free access to lump sums. Banks hold your money. Circles make you keep it.

**11/** Sources: Gugerty, *You Can't Save Alone* (J. Development Economics, 2007);
